Repository files navigation # Server-Sent Events (SSE) Demo with FastAPI [Permalink: Server-Sent Events (SSE) Demo with FastAPI](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#server-sent-events-sse-demo-with-fastapi) This is a simple demonstration of Server-Sent Events (SSE) using FastAPI. It provides a minimalistic frontend that displays real-time updates from the server in a table format. ## Table of Contents [Permalink: Table of Contents](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#table-of-contents) - [Overview](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#overview) - [Installation](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#installation) - [Usage](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#usage) - [License](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#license) ## Overview [Permalink: Overview](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#overview) Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a web technology that allows servers to push real-time updates to web clients over a single HTTP connection. In this project, we use FastAPI to create a simple SSE server and provide a frontend for visualizing the real-time updates. ## Installation [Permalink: Installation](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#installation) 1. Clone the repository to your local machine: ``` git clone https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse.git ``` 2. Navigate to the project directory: ``` cd sse-fastapi-demo ``` 3. Install the required Python dependencies using `poetry`: ``` poetry install ``` ## Usage [Permalink: Usage](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#usage) 1. Start the FastAPI application: ``` uvicorn main:app --reload ``` The application will be accessible at [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000/). 2. Open a web browser and visit [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000/) to see the SSE demo in action. The page will display real-time updates in a table format. ## License [Permalink: License](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#license) This project is licensed under the MIT License - see the [LICENSE](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse/blob/main/LICENSE) file for details. ## About This is a simple demonstration of Server-Sent Events (SSE) using FastAPI. It provides a minimalistic frontend that displays real-time updates from the server in a table format. ### Topics [python](https://github.com/topics/python "Topic: python") [demo](https://github.com/topics/demo "Topic: demo") [real-time](https://github.com/topics/real-time "Topic: real-time") [server-sent-events](https://github.com/topics/server-sent-events "Topic: server-sent-events") [event-streaming](https://github.com/topics/event-streaming "Topic: event-streaming") [fastapi](https://github.com/topics/fastapi "Topic: fastapi") ### Resources [Readme](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#readme-ov-file) ### License [MIT license](https://github.com/AndreyKlychnikov/fastapi-sse#MIT-1-ov-file) ### Uh oh! ### Example Code
```
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world() -> AsyncIterable[str]:
raise HTTPException(status_code=501, detail="This endpoint is not yet implemented")
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield char
```
Also tried this but it raises `TypeError: 'coroutine' object is not iterable` which is explained by [this](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L492).
```
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
app = FastAPI()
@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world() -> EventSourceResponse:
# raise HTTPException(status_code=501, detail="This endpoint is not yet implemented")
async def _hello_world_generator():
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
return EventSourceResponse(_hello_world_generator())
```
### Description
When using `EventSourceResponse` with FastAPI, the endpoint function effectively becomes a generator-based streaming endpoint.
Reference:
- [https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L526](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L526)
### Problem
In production systems, streaming endpoints frequently require pre-stream logic.
These steps may legitimately raise `HTTPException` or other exceptions that are mapped to exception handlers.
### Desired behavior
If an exception occurs before the streaming response begins, it would be preferable for FastAPI to return a standard HTTP error response (e.g., `JSONResponse` from the default `HTTPException` handler).
This maintains a clean separation between:
- Normal request errors (returned as standard HTTP responses)
- Errors occurring during an active stream (which must be communicated through the stream protocol)
### Rationale
From an API design perspective, errors that occur prior to emitting the first stream chunk are still part of the normal request lifecycle and should follow the usual HTTP error semantics.
Once the stream begins (headers sent + body streaming), error handling must follow streaming semantics (SSE error events).
Separating these two phases helps avoid ambiguous responses and aligns better with how HTTP streaming works.
### Proposal
This is a rough idea and may not be the correct implementation approach.
Introduce an additional check around [https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L528](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L528).
If the resolved response class is `EventSourceResponse`, the endpoint function could first be executed **as a normal coroutine**. Any exceptions raised during this phase would propagate through FastAPI’s standard exception handling flow.
If execution succeeds, the returned async generator could then be extracted, after which the SSE stream would proceed as usual.

Thanks for detailed write-up. This is a very common scenario when dealing with streaming responses in Python and ASGI frameworks.
The issue you're experiencing with the "generator trap" (where pre-stream exceptions aren't raised until iteration begins) is tied to how Python generators work.
Fortunately, your second approach (separating the pre-stream logic from the generator) is exactly the right mental model! The reason it raised a `TypeError` is due to a clash with the response\_class argument when you are already returning a custom Response instance directly.
When you return a Response object (like `EventSourceResponse`) directly from the endpoint, you should remove `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the `@app.get` decorator.
Here is the corrected, idiomatic way to achieve exactly what you want: clean HTTP exceptions before the stream, and standard SSE behavior after.
```
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
# Assuming you are using sse_starlette (FastAPI doesn't have fastapi.sse built-in)
from sse_starlette.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent
app = FastAPI()
# 1. REMOVE response_class=EventSourceResponse from the decorator
@app.get("/hello")
async def hello_world():
# 2. Pre-stream logic runs synchronously here.
# This will correctly return a standard JSON HTTP 501 response!
raise HTTPException(status_code=501, detail="This endpoint is not yet implemented")
# 3. Define the async generator for the stream
async def _hello_world_generator():
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)

# 4. Return the instantiated Response object directly
return EventSourceResponse(_hello_world_generator())
```
Why this solves your problem:
Because `hello_world` no longer contains a yield in its outer scope, `FastAPI` evaluates it as a standard coroutine immediately upon request. Any `HTTPException` raised here is caught by FastAPI's standard exception handlers and returned as normal JSON. If no exception is raised, it instantiates and returns the `EventSourceResponse`, which FastAPI will then stream seamlessly.
Because this pattern fully handles the separation of "normal request errors" vs "active stream errors" without requiring modifications to FastAPI's core routing logic, a change to `fastapi/routing.py` is likely not necessary.
Hope this helps! Let me know if you run into any other issues. | BetaWas this translation helpful? * * *
## Why pre-stream exceptions are silently lost
When your endpoint is an async generator (`async def … yield …`), Python does **not** execute the function body when the endpoint is called. It returns a generator object immediately. The body only runs when FastAPI starts iterating the generator to stream data — at that point HTTP headers (`200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`) have already been sent to the client, so there is no way to send an HTTP error response.
```
# BAD — raise before yield never fires at request time
@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world() -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
raise HTTPException(status_code=501) # ← runs during iteration, not on request
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
```
* * *
## Solution 1 — FastAPI Dependency (recommended)
Dependencies are resolved **synchronously before** the generator is created, so `HTTPException` raised there works exactly like on any normal endpoint:
```
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent
app = FastAPI()
async def check_access():
"""Raise HTTPException here to block the stream before it starts."""
authorized = False # your real check here
if not authorized:
raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")
@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world(
_: None = Depends(check_access),
) -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
```
A `GET /hello` with failing auth → **403 JSON response**, never touches the generator.
* * *
## Solution 2 — Separate pre-stream logic from the generator
If your pre-stream logic needs the same scope as the generator (e.g. a DB connection), keep them in the same function but separate the non-generator part:
```
@app.get("/hello")
async def hello_world():
# Everything here runs synchronously on the request
authorized = False # your real check
if not authorized:
raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")
async def _stream() -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
for char in "Hello, World!":
yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
# Return the EventSourceResponse directly (no response_class on the decorator)
return EventSourceResponse(_stream())
```
Note: when you return `EventSourceResponse(...)` directly, omit `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the decorator — FastAPI only needs that decorator argument when the endpoint itself is the async generator.
* * *
**TL;DR**: use a `Depends()` for pre-stream validation — that is the idiomatic FastAPI pattern and requires zero changes to your generator logic. | BetaWas this translation helpful? # Real-Time Notifications in Python: Using SSE with FastAPI

[![İnan DELİBAŞ](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*KP1k0wsMHc4pcnpckF0q1A.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@inandelibas?source=post_page---byline--1c8c54746eb7---------------------------------------)

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*RmUX86awAwNKOsSFxj6hcA.png)

Modern web applications increasingly rely on real-time updates, such as live chat, dashboards, and notifications. Users expect instantaneous feedback (such as new messages, alerts, and data streams) without having to refresh manually. Traditional request/response isn’t sufficient for this, so “push” technologies are crucial. Server-Sent Events (SSE) offer one such solution, enabling the server to push updates to the client over HTTP, thereby eliminating the need for the client to poll.

> _✨_ [_See full project on GitHub_](https://github.com/inanpy/fastapi-sse-example)

## What Are Server-Sent Events (SSE)?

Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a **browser-native** API (part of HTML5) for unidirectional server→client streaming. In SSE, the client opens a persistent HTTP connection (with Accept: **text/event-stream**), and the server continues to send text messages over that channel. Unlike WebSockets, the channel is **_one-way_**: the server pushes data, and the client listens. The EventSource API in JavaScript handles the connection and parses incoming events. Each message is sent as plain text, e.g., data: …\\n\\n, and the browser dispatches it as an event. SSE also supports optional fields (e.g., event:, id:) to label events or resume streams.

For example:

```
event: ping
id: 123
data: {"time": "2025-06-12T11:30:00Z"}
```

## SSE vs WebSockets vs Polling: What Should You Use?

- **Long-Polling:** The client repeatedly sends requests asking for new data. It’s inefficient but straightforward: most requests return no new data. It adds latency (each poll waits) and loads the server with constant new connections.
- **SSE:** Ideal for _one-way_ streaming from the server to many clients. It’s easy to implement (just set Content-Type: text/event-stream and stream chunks), works over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, and auto-reconnects if dropped. SSE saves bandwidth by using a single long-lived connection rather than making frequent polls. However, it can’t send messages from the client to the server.
- **WebSockets** provide full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single TCP connection. It’s best for chat apps, multiplayer games, or any scenario where both the client and server need to send messages. However, WebSockets require more setup and specialized server support, and may not traverse proxies as easily. They also maintain more overhead per connection (though still efficient). In practice, choose SSE for simple **server→client updates** (notifications, live feeds) and WebSockets when you need client→server streaming or lower latency two-way communication.

> _SSE is ideal for low-frequency, one-way updates like notifications or status changes. It’s lightweight and easy to implement. For high-frequency or bidirectional communication, WebSockets provide better scalability and lower latency under load._

## How Server-Sent Events Work Under the Hood

Underneath, SSE is just **chunked HTTP streaming**. The client makes a standard HTTP GET with Accept: text/event-stream, and the server responds with headers like:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache
Connection: keep-alive
```

Then **keeps the connection open** indefinitely. Each event is sent as UTF-8 text. Single newlines separate fields in an event (such as data or event), and a **blank line (\\n\\n) ends each event**. For example:

```
data: {"price": 123.45}
data: USD
id: 42
```

Here \\n\\n after the id: 42 signals the event is complete. The TCP connection remains open (no final 0-length chunk is sent), and the server can later write more chunks as new events occur. Because HTTP/1.1 supports _persistent connections_ and _chunked transfer encoding_, the server doesn’t need to know the content length in advance. SSE runs entirely over standard HTTP ports (80/443), allowing it to pass through firewalls without special configuration.

The browser uses the EventSource interface to parse these chunks into message events. It also handles **automatic reconnection**: if the connection drops, the browser retries by default, even sending the Last-Event-ID header if the last message had an ID. This lets the server resume the stream without duplicating messages. In short, SSE cleverly transforms HTTP’s request-response model into a continuous one-way data stream.

## SSE in Python: The Benefits and the Challenges

In Python, **SSE’s** HTTP-based nature is both a benefit and a challenge. On the plus side, you can use any web framework to stream **text responses** and set the Content-Type header to **text/event-stream**. No special protocol (such as WebSocket) is required, and existing HTTP servers (including ASGI frameworks like **FastAPI** or even **WSGI** with some adjustments) can handle it. SSE is lightweight, stateless, and typically easier to test than WebSockets. Libraries like **sse-starlette** provide helpers, and Python’s async features (asyncio, FastAPI/Starlette) make streaming straightforward.

On the **downside**, SSE is unidirectional (server→client only), so it can’t replace cases where the client must push data (like chat input). Python’s typical WSGI servers (e.g., Gunicorn in sync mode) may not stream well, so you often need ASGI servers (Uvicorn, Daphne) or disable buffering. Additionally, maintaining multiple HTTP connections open consumes resources (although SSE is more efficient than polling, each open connection still utilizes a socket and memory). Concurrency must be managed; for example, in a multi-process server, one process may not see updates from another unless shared storage (such as Redis or a database) is used. The client-side reconnection and “Last-Event-ID” logic must also be handled: if events have an “id” field, the browser will automatically include it on reconnect. Overall, SSE in Python works best when you structure your app asynchronously or dedicate a worker to the SSE stream.

## When to Use SSE Instead of WebSockets

Use SSE when your application primarily needs **server→client push** of events, and the client doesn’t need to send frequent data back. Typical scenarios include live notifications, news feeds, real-time dashboards, or any situation where the server initiates updates. SSE is simpler to implement in these cases (no handshake, uses HTTP) and integrates easily with HTTP caching and authentication. For instance, a notifications service where the server tells the client, “You have a new alert,” is a perfect SSE use-case.

> In contrast, if you need full **bi-directional** streaming (where the client sends data back, such as in chat or gaming) or extremely **low latency**, WebSockets may be a **better** option. In summary, **SSE excels for “one-way” real-time streams**, while WebSockets are better suited for **two-way** or **high-throughput** needs.

## Use Case: Live Notifications

### Building a Real-Time Notification System in FastAPI

A typical SSE use case is a push **notification system**. For example, when a significant event occurs on the backend (such as a new message, system alert, or status change), you want all connected clients to be notified immediately. One approach is to have clients connect to an SSE endpoint (e.g., /notifications/) and have backend processes publish events to that endpoint’s stream.

In FastAPI, you might write an endpoint like **/subscribe/{user\_id}** that keeps a stream open for that user. Meanwhile, whenever something happens (e.g., a background task completes or a database record updates), you publish an event to a shared broker (such as Redis). The SSE endpoint’s async generator listens on that broker and yields incoming messages. A simplified sketch:

```
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import aioredis, asyncio, json

app = FastAPI()
redis = await aioredis.from_url("redis://localhost")

async def notification_stream(user_id: str):
    pubsub = redis.pubsub()
    await pubsub.subscribe("notifications")
    while True:
        msg = await pubsub.get_message(ignore_subscribe_messages=True)
        if msg and msg["type"] == "message":
            event = json.loads(msg["data"])
            # filter by user_id if needed...
            yield f"data: {json.dumps(event)}\n\n"
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)

@app.get("/notifications/{user_id}")
async def notifications(user_id: str):
    return StreamingResponse(notification_stream(user_id), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

On the backend, any part of the app (or a Celery task) can publish to Redis:

```
await redis.publish("notifications", json.dumps({"user": user_id, "text": "New alert!"}))
```

Then all clients subscribed via SSE will immediately receive that JSON. This pub/sub pattern is familiar; one guide notes using Redis pub/sub for precisely this purpose. You can also push events via other brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka) or use a task queue (Celery) that, upon completion, calls redis.publish().

> _💻 You can find a complete working example of this structure on GitHub:_
>
> _👉_ [_https://github.com/inanpy/fastapi-sse-example_](https://github.com/inanpy/fastapi-sse-example)

## SSE Performance Tips for High-Traffic Apps

- **Compression:** SSE streams are text-based, so you can (and should) enable gzip/deflate compression on your HTTP response. This can cut bandwidth by 70–90% for typical JSON payloads. Most web servers (e.g., nginx, uvicorn) support HTTP compression; ensure that the Content-Type: text/event-stream is compressible according to your configuration.
- **Minimal Data:** Keep SSE messages small. Only send the data the client needs. Since each event uses one HTTP packet over TCP, minimizing payload improves throughput.
- **Batching Events:** If events occur rapidly, consider batching multiple data items into a single SSE event (as a JSON array) rather than sending many back-to-back events. This reduces overhead (each event has some framing bytes).
- **Disable Buffering:** Many reverse proxies (nginx, UWSGI) buffer responses by default, which defeats streaming. Disable buffering for SSE endpoints. For example, send the header X-Accel-Buffering: no (nginx) or configure proxy\_buffering off. This ensures each yield is flushed to the client immediately.
- **Close Idle Streams:** Always close SSE connections on the client side when they are no longer in use (to free server resources). On the server side, if you detect the client disconnect (e.g., GeneratorExit in Python), stop sending—unused open connections waste memory and file descriptors. Many examples explicitly check for broken clients and break the loop, or rely on async frameworks to cancel the generator.
- **Connection Limits (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2):** In HTTP/1.1, browsers typically allow only ~6 concurrent connections per origin. If your app must serve many SSE clients, use HTTP/2. With HTTP/2, a single TCP connection can multiplex dozens or hundreds of streams. Deploying your app on a server (or proxy) that supports HTTP/2 will greatly increase scalability.

## Handling Multiple Clients and Scaling with ASGI Servers

To serve **multiple** concurrent SSE clients, use an ASGI server such as Uvicorn. This can handle asynchronous I/O efficiently. You can run multiple worker processes (or threads), but remember that each SSE stream lives in one process. If your application uses multiple processes (e.g., via Gunicorn workers), ensure that the event source (Redis or whatever) is shared; otherwise, one process won’t see events published in another. A good approach is to maintain a single central Pub/Sub (e.g., Redis, Kafka) that all processes subscribe to. Then, each instance streams to its clients independently.

If you need to broadcast to **all clients**, consider a pub/sub or message queue: publish an event once, have every server instance send it to its connected clients. Libraries like **sse-starlette** help manage multiple channels. Also, ensure you test your deployment. For high-scale applications, you may need **load balancers** or **sticky sessions** if clients are pinned to particular servers, or use **global pub/sub** so that any instance can serve any client.

## What to Watch Out for in Production (Timeouts, Keep-Alive, CORS)

- **Proxy Timeouts:** Be aware of reverse proxy settings. Many proxies (nginx, AWS ELB, etc.) will terminate idle streams after a timeout (often 60 seconds). To prevent this, either send periodic comment heartbeats (e.g., “: heartbeat\\n\\n”) or adjust the proxy’s keepalive/timeout settings. For nginx, you can set proxy\_read\_timeout to a high value or use X-Accel-Buffering: no as above.
- **CORS and Authentication:** If your SSE endpoint is on a different origin or requires auth, configure CORS and credentials properly. In JS, you can create a new EventSource(url, { withCredentials: true }) to send cookies. On the server, set allow\_origins and allow\_credentials if using middleware (e.g., FastAPI’s CORSMiddleware). Ensure TLS (HTTPS) is used if credentials are involved.
- **Connection Limits:** As noted, browsers limit the number of concurrent connections per domain. Avoid using too many SSE connections on a single page; instead, consider splitting them across subdomains or using HTTP/2. Test in all target browsers.
- **DNS/IP Blocking:** Some CDNs or firewalls may treat long-lived HTTP connections unusually. Ensure your hosting environment supports streaming responses (some servers that buffer or require Content-Length may not work).
- **Resource Usage:** Each SSE client uses one server thread or coroutine. For a large-scale system, monitor the open connection count and memory usage. It may be necessary to run on servers optimized for I/O (async) and to increase limits on file descriptors.

## In Conclusion;

**SSE** remains a **simple and effective** tool for **real-time notifications**. It’s built on standard **HTTP**, widely supported, and ideal for unidirectional data streams. For many use cases, such as live alerts, feeds, and dashboards, SSE provides a lightweight alternative to more complex WebSocket setups. The trade-offs are now well understood: SSE excels at server→client updates with automatic reconnection, but isn’t bidirectional. When you need a **straightforward push mechanism** (and especially when you can leverage Python’s async frameworks), SSE is still a very relevant choice.

We have mature tooling: **FastAPI** and libraries like **sse-starlette** make building SSE streams easy. And for developers, SSE means handling real-time without leaving the comfort of HTTP. In short, SSE’s **one-way streaming model** remains useful, bridging classic web protocols and modern real-time user experiences.

## Final Thoughts

Real-time capabilities are no longer a luxury — they’re a **core expectation** in modern web experiences. Whether you’re building a live dashboard, sending instant alerts, or updating a user’s feed, the ability to push updates seamlessly can transform how users interact with your application.

**Server-Sent Events (SSE)** offers a **robust, elegant, and underrated** approach to real-time communication. It’s easy to implement with **FastAPI**, integrates smoothly into existing HTTP infrastructures, and shines in scenarios where the data flow is **one-way** from server to client.

If your use case doesn’t demand bidirectional communication, **SSE should be your default starting point**, before jumping into the complexity of **WebSockets**.

Have you implemented real-time features using **SSE** in your projects?

I’d love to hear your thoughts, lessons, or questions in the comments.

If this article helped you, consider sharing it with your developer network or giving it a **few claps** 👏

### Example Code
```
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse
from models import Event
@router.get("/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def stream(request, service) -> AsyncIterable[Event]:
listener = await service.register_listener()
offset = listener.offset
try:
while True:
if await request.is_disconnected():
break
event = await service.get_next_event(offset)
if event:
offset += 1
yield event
finally:
await service.unregister_listener()
```
### Description
Currently, the Server-Sent Events (SSE) implementation in FastAPI uses internal constants:
```
fastapi.sse._PING_INTERVAL: float = 15.0
fastapi.sse.KEEPALIVE_COMMENT = b": ping\n\n"
```
These values are not configurable, which makes it difficult to:
- adjust keepalive frequency for different infrastructure setups (e.g. proxies, load balancers)
- tune behavior for long-lived connections
- comply with environments that require custom heartbeat intervals or formats
### Additional context
In the current implementation, the keepalive comment is sent as:
```
b": ping\n\n"
```
However, in Google Chrome DevTools (EventStream tab), this is not recognized as an event, and the connection may silently drop without any visible activity.
In my case, I had to change it to:
```
b"event: ping\ndata: null\n\n"
```
so that it is properly visible as an event in the browser.
Additionally, the default ping interval of 15 seconds is not sufficient for my use case, and I needed to reduce it to 5 seconds to keep connections alive reliably.
At the moment, the only way to achieve this is by overriding internal FastAPI constants, which is not ideal.
It would be beneficial if both the ping interval and keepalive format were configurable in a clean and supported way (e.g., via EventSourceResponse parameters), instead of relying on modifying internal implementation details.
